findings.suggestion: Hash outside the transaction: make signUp() non-transactional, compute the hash, then call a small @Transactional insert method (separate bean, so the proxy applies). Alternatively set spring.datasource.hikari.auto-commit=false with spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.connection.provider_disables_autocommit=true so acquisition is genuinely lazy — but that is a protected-path config edit and does not remove the CPU cost from the request. Either way, size the pool explicitly. Confirm before/after by counting rows in pg_stat_activity with state='idle in transaction' during a sign-up burst, and by HikariCP's connection-acquisition timer.
findings.summary: signUp() is @Transactional and computes the Argon2id hash (m=16384 KiB, t=2, ~25 ms) as the first thing inside the transaction, before any statement is issued. With Hikari's default autoCommit=true, Hibernate acquires the JDBC connection at transaction begin (to turn autocommit off) rather than at first statement, so a pool connection sits idle-in-transaction for the whole hash. application.yml sets no spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size, so the pool is the default 10 and is shared with the redirect cache-miss path. At 60 sign-ups/min/IP the aggregate is bounded only by the number of source addresses: ~400 sign-ups/s in flight would hold all 10 connections, and the endpoint that starves is the click path's PostgreSQL fallback.

findings.suggestion: Bound concurrent hashing rather than the per-IP rate: wrap PasswordHasher.hash/matches in a Semaphore sized to something like the core count (queue or 503 beyond it), or cap server.tomcat.threads.max so the worst case is arithmetic somebody has checked. Confirm with a heap/allocation profile under a concurrent sign-up burst and by asserting the deployed -Xmx against threads × 16 MiB.
findings.summary: Nothing bounds the number of concurrent Argon2id hashes. Each one allocates 16 MiB; Tomcat's default max-threads is 200 and no thread cap or heap size is configured in this repository, so 200 concurrent sign-ups is ~3.2 GiB of transient allocation plus 200 threads of memory-hard CPU. The per-IP SIGN_UP bucket (60/min) bounds one caller, not aggregate concurrency, and the limiter fails open when Redis is unreachable (RedisTokenBucketRateLimiter, allow-on-exception), so during a Redis outage this endpoint is unmetered. Sign-in already carried this exposure and it predates the change; sign-up adds a second entry point on the same key with the same bucket, roughly doubling it.

findings.suggestion: Put `SET lock_timeout = '3s';` at the top of the migration so it fails fast and is retried rather than head-of-line blocking reads, and run it in a low-traffic window. Confirm by checking pg_locks for the granted/waiting chain on links while it applies in staging.
findings.summary: ALTER TABLE links ALTER COLUMN customer_id DROP NOT NULL is catalog-only and instant, but it needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on links — the table the redirect path reads on every cache miss. With no lock_timeout set, the ALTER queues behind any in-flight query on links and, while it waits, every later query on links queues behind it. On a busy instance that turns a millisecond of DDL into a stall of the hot path for as long as the longest running query, during a deploy, with Flyway blocking startup behind it.

findings.suggestion: Make it partial: CREATE INDEX ... ON links (customer_id, created_at DESC, code ASC) WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL, as a separate migration once anonymous volume is known. Confirm with pg_relation_size on the index and a count of NULL-owner rows after a few weeks.
findings.summary: ix_links_owner_listing (customer_id, created_at DESC, code ASC) now carries anonymous rows for the first time: a btree indexes NULLs, and every anonymous link adds an entry under a leading NULL that no query can ever match, because findOwnedBy and findByDomainAndCodeAndCustomerId are equality-scoped. The migration comment says the index 'never serves an anonymous row', which is true of reads and not of writes — the insert cost, index size and vacuum work are all paid. Magnitude depends entirely on anonymous volume, which nobody has measured; at low volume this is invisible.

findings.suggestion: Either accept it and instrument it (alert on the count of rows WHERE customer_id IS NULL and on the ANONYMOUS_CREATE 429 rate), or add a reaper that hard-deletes anonymous rows some margin past expires_at — noting that reissuing their codes is explicitly forbidden, so a reaper needs a tombstone. Decide before ship rather than after the table is large.
findings.summary: Anonymous rows accumulate without bound and nothing removes them. Expiry is derived at read time and nothing sweeps, so an expired anonymous link keeps its row, its index entries and its (domain, code) namespace slot forever, and no owner exists who could delete it. The only ceiling is the ANONYMOUS_CREATE bucket at 30/min per source address — which is per-IP, not global, and fails open when Redis is unreachable. I cannot say from the code how fast the table will grow; the honest statement is that the growth rate is set by attacker choice rather than by anything in this service.

findings.suggestion: Move invalidateBeforeIssuing outside the transactional boundary (commit the row, then invalidate, then respond — the 503-on-failure semantics can be preserved by doing it in the controller or a wrapper bean), or explicitly size the pool for the slow-Redis case. Confirm by holding Redis at a 1s delay and watching HikariCP pending-connection count.
findings.summary: createAnonymous holds the database transaction open across a Redis round trip: resolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing(code) runs inside @Transactional, after saveAndFlush. Redis timeouts are 1s connect and 1s read, so a Redis brownout parks a pool connection for up to ~2s per request. With the default pool of 10 and an unauthenticated caller supplying the traffic, a slow (not dead) Redis converts into connection-pool exhaustion for everything else, including the redirect cache-miss path. This mirrors the existing create() exactly — the pattern is pre-existing — but it is newly reachable without a credential.

findings.suggestion: If it is ever worth touching: build the candidate list and ask once (existsByHostIn(candidates)), and skip the parent walk entirely when the canonical host is a dotted quad.
findings.summary: isListed issues one existsByHost query per parent label, inside the create transaction — four to six round trips for an ordinary hostname. Newly, HostNormalizer canonicalises numeric hosts to dotted quads, so an IP target now walks 127.0.0.1 -> 0.0.1 -> 0.1 -> 1: four queries whose answers cannot be meaningful, on both create paths. Each is a unique-index hit on a tiny table, so the cost is round trips, not work; create is not the hot path and this is a rounding error at any load this service will plausibly see.

findings.suggestion: Note the expected build time against the production row count in the approval for this protected-path migration. If customers is ever large, split it out as a non-transactional Flyway migration using CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
findings.summary: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX (not CONCURRENTLY, and Flyway wraps the migration in a transaction so CONCURRENTLY is not available without configuring it) takes a SHARE lock on customers for the duration of the build, blocking writes — i.e. sign-ups and nothing else, since sign-in only reads. Harmless at the current table size; worth knowing it scales with the customer count, which self-service sign-up is the thing that makes grow.

findings.suggestion: Implement Persistable<UUID> with a transient isNew flag on the entities, or inject EntityManager and call persist() directly. Confirm with hibernate SQL logging on a single sign-up: two statements today, one after.
findings.summary: CustomerEntity has an application-assigned UUID id, no @Version and does not implement Persistable, so Spring Data's isNew() sees a non-null id and routes saveAndFlush through merge() — Hibernate issues a SELECT by primary key before the INSERT. One wasted round trip per sign-up. The same is true of every link insert, so this is a pre-existing house pattern rather than something this change introduced.

not_examined: The redirect hot path itself (RedirectController, LinkResolver, ResolutionCache, RedisClickCounter, ClickFlushJob) — read to confirm it is untouched by this change, but not reviewed as new work; the impact analysis's claim that anonymous links traverse it identically checks out (CachedLink carries no customerId).

Hibernate's actual connection-acquisition timing. PERF-1 assumes eager acquisition at transaction begin, which is the behaviour with Hikari autoCommit=true and no provider_disables_autocommit; I did not verify it by running the service with DEBUG on the pool.
redis/token_bucket.lua — the limiter's Redis-side cost and key expiry were not read.
Query plans. No EXPLAIN was run against any statement; index coverage was read off the migrations only.
Deployment resource limits. There is no Dockerfile, k8s manifest or JVM flag anywhere in this repository, so heap size, CPU allocation and replica count in PERF-2 are unknown rather than assumed.

Real traffic volumes and mix. Nothing here says how many redirects, creates or sign-ups per second to expect, so every 'at what load' statement in the findings is arithmetic from configured limits, not from measurement.
Test-suite runtime and the Testcontainers changes in AbstractIntegrationTest/AbstractRestartIntegrationTest — CI cost, not service performance.
Allocation behaviour of IDN.toASCII and the split-based label walk in HostNormalizer; judged trivially small on a non-hot path and not profiled.
summary: The redirect path — the one that matters — is untouched: no new work, no extra round trip, no analytics write added to it, and the (domain, code) unique index still backs the only lookup it makes. Anonymous links flow through it identically. Nothing in this change makes a click slower. What the change does add is two unauthenticated write endpoints in front of a database pool that has never been sized (Hikari default 10) and a memory-hard hash with no concurrency bound. The three findings worth a human are: sign-up holds a pool connection idle through ~25 ms of Argon2 (PERF-1); nothing caps concurrent Argon2 at 16 MiB apiece against a 200-thread connector (PERF-2); and V4's ALTER TABLE takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on links, the table the click path falls back to, with no lock_timeout (PERF-3). The rest is smaller: an index that now stores rows it can never serve, anonymous rows that accumulate with no reaper, a transaction held across a Redis call on the new path. None of it is measured — nobody has run this under load — so severities reflect the cost when it goes wrong and confidence reflects how much the code alone can prove.
